lessons.title: Man-to-man basics
lessons.objective: Describe man defense, closeouts and denying the pass.

payload.prompt: What does man-to-man defense mean?

options.text: Each defender is responsible for guarding one specific opponent, moving with them around the court.
All defenders guard the ball and leave the post open.
Defenders guard areas of the court instead of specific players.

explanation.correct: Right. Man-to-man is the most basic defense: you guard your person, they guard theirs. Follow your player everywhere.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Man-to-man means each defender is assigned one opponent and guards them all over the court. This is fundamental basketball defense.

payload.prompt: What does it mean to deny the pass?

options.text: Playing tight on your opponent to make it hard for them to receive a pass from a teammate.
Stealing the ball every time it is passed.
Leaving your opponent open on purpose.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Denying the pass means staying close enough that your opponent cannot easily catch a pass. It is a fundamental defensive principle.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. To deny the pass, you play tight on your opponent, making it difficult for their teammates to get them the ball.

payload.prompt: What is a closeout?

options.text: Sprinting at a shooter who just received a pass, trying to contest without fouling.
Guarding someone in the paint.
Ending the game after the final basket.

explanation.correct: Right. A closeout is a quick, controlled rush at a shooter to contest the shot without fouling. Speed and control both matter.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A closeout is when you sprint at a shooter after they catch the ball to try to block or contest the shot without making contact.

payload.prompt: Match each defensive action to what it does.

pairs.definition: Guarding the player with the ball, trying to prevent them from scoring, passing or driving.
Playing tight on your opponent so teammates cannot easily pass them the ball.
Sprinting at a shooter to contest the shot after they receive a pass.

distractorDefinitions: Staying under the basket to block shots.
Pressing full court from baseline to baseline.

explanation.summary: On-ball is primary defense; deny keeps the ball away; closeout contests shots from range.

payload.question: What is she complimenting?

options.text: The defenders guarding the ball handler are playing excellent, physical, tightly.
The team only guards the person with the ball.
They are on the ball in the paint.
The team is fouling everyone.

payload.translation: She means the team's defenders are playing great defense on whoever has the ball, making it hard to pass or shoot.

followUps.why: You recognize that good on-ball defense means tight, aggressive play on the ball handler.

followUps.line: Does that help their defense everywhere?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking whether strong on-ball play helps the whole team.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: On-ball defense is just playing good defense on the person with the ball.

lessons.title: Help defense and rotations
lessons.objective: Read who helps, who rotates and who is left open.

payload.prompt: What is help defense?

options.text: A defender leaving their assigned opponent to stop a drive or penetration by another player.
Passing the ball to a teammate who is open.
A player on the bench coming into the game to substitute.

explanation.correct: Right. Help defense stops penetration by having an extra defender collapse on the ball handler. This leaves someone else open.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Help defense is when a defender leaves their own player to stop a penetrating ball handler, knowing it creates a gap elsewhere.

payload.prompt: What happens when a help defender leaves their player?

options.text: Another defender must rotate over to guard the open player, creating a chain of moves.
The offense stops moving the ball.
That open player automatically scores.

explanation.correct: Exactly. When help defense leaves an opponent, the rotation means another defender slides over to cover that gap. Good rotations stop easy buckets.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rotation is the chain of defenders sliding over after help defense creates a gap. Each defender covers someone else in sequence.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Their help defense is too slow.

payload.question: What is she noticing?

options.text: The defense is not rotating fast enough when help is needed, leaving gaps open.
A player is too slow to run down the court.
The coaching staff is not helping.
They are not scoring fast enough.

payload.translation: She means when defenders try to help on drives, the rotation is sluggish and opposing players get open looks because the movement is delayed.

followUps.line: Yeah, they get beat on penetration.
followUps.why: You recognize that slow help defense leads to easy offensive scoring.
A good follow-up asking whether poor communication is causing the defensive breakdowns.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Help defense needs to be quick and coordinated, or the offense punishes it.

lessons.title: Zone defense and how to beat it
lessons.objective: Describe 2-3, 3-2, 1-3-1 and matchup zones and where the gaps live.

payload.prompt: Match each zone to its formation.

pairs.definition: Two defenders at the top guarding the perimeter and three at the baseline guarding the paint. Most common zone.
Three defenders across the top and two at the baseline, protecting against perimeter shooting.
One defender at the top, three in the middle and one on the baseline. Often used as a trapping zone.

explanation.summary: 2-3 is most common; 3-2 stops shooters; 1-3-1 traps and disrupts.

payload.prompt: In a 2-3 zone, tap where the gap between the two top defenders is (the hardest place to guard).

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing zone defense gaps.

explanation.correct: Right! The top of the 2-3 zone has a gap where the two defenders meet, and swing passes can exploit it.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. The biggest gap in a 2-3 zone is where the two top defenders meet at half court. Offenses try to hit that seam.

payload.prompt: How should an offense attack a zone defense?

options.text: Move the ball around the perimeter to find gaps and shoot open threes or make short passes into the paint.
Drive into the heart of the zone and try to score.
Stay still and wait for an open shot.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Ball movement makes zones shift and creates gaps. Three-pointers and passes into soft spots beat zones.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Zones are beaten by good ball movement and perimeter shooting. The more the ball moves, the harder it is for zone defenders.

payload.prompt: What is a matchup zone?

options.text: A hybrid zone where defenders guard an area but also account for nearby opponents, blending zone and man-to-man principles.
Defending players based only on height.
A zone that never changes formation.

explanation.correct: Right. Matchup zones give defenders flexibility: they have a zone to cover but can guard nearby opponents like man-to-man.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A matchup zone blends zone principles (guarding an area) with man-to-man principles (accounting for nearby opponents).

lessons.title: Rebounding and the box-out
lessons.objective: Explain boxing out, offensive boards and why rebounds swing games.

payload.prompt: What is a box-out?

options.text: Using your body to shield an opponent from the rebound, standing between them and the basket.
Throwing the ball out of bounds.
Arguing with the referee about a call.

explanation.correct: Right. A box-out puts your body between your opponent and the basket. This gives you a better chance at the rebound.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Boxing out is a fundamental rebounding skill: you use your body to keep an opponent away from the basket so you can get the rebound.

payload.prompt: Why are offensive rebounds valuable?

options.text: They give the shooting team another possession without losing the ball, giving a second chance to score.
They count as two points instead of one.
They end the shot clock and reset everything.

explanation.correct: Exactly. An offensive rebound is a second chance: if you miss but grab the board, you get the ball back for another shot.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Offensive rebounds give the offensive team a second possession without turning the ball over. They are highly valuable possessions.

payload.prompt: What are second-chance points?

options.text: Points scored after an offensive rebound on a second shot attempt from the same missed shot.
Points scored by the team with the second-best record.
Free throws after a missed shot.

explanation.correct: Right. Second-chance points come after offensive rebounds. They swing games because you get to shoot again.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Second-chance points are scored after an offensive rebound, giving a team another attempt at the basket.

payload.prompt: A shot is missed and the shooting team's player grabs the ball before it goes out. Is this an offensive rebound?

scene.alt: A player grabbing a rebound on their team's miss.

explanation.correct: Correct. The shooting team grabbing a miss is an offensive rebound. They get the ball back for another shot.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. If the team that shot the ball gets the rebound on a miss, that is an offensive rebound.

payload.prompt: A defender stands between an opponent and the basket when a shot goes up. Is this a box-out?

scene.alt: A defender positioning between opponent and basket.

choices.label: No, this is just standing there.

explanation.correct: Right. A box-out starts the moment a shot goes up. Good position gives you the rebound.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. If you are between your opponent and the basket on a shot, you are attempting to box them out for the rebound.

payload.prompt: What percentage of missed shots does a star rebounder typically grab when on the court?

explanation.correct: Right around there. Elite rebounders get about 25-35% of missed shots on the court, which is huge.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A great rebounder typically grabs 25-35% of available rebounds when playing. That is elite-level rebounding.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They are killing us on the boards.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The opponent is dominating rebounding, getting offensive boards and second-chance points.
The opponent is fouling a lot.
The opponent is yelling at their coaching staff.
The opponent is sitting on the bench.

payload.translation: The other team is winning the rebounding battle, getting multiple possessions and extra chances to score through offensive boards.

followUps.line: Yeah, they are getting every miss.
followUps.why: You recognize that poor rebounding means the other team gets second chances.

followUps.line: We need to box out better.
followUps.why: A good follow-up identifying the rebounding technique needed to stop it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Losing the boards means the other team gets extra possessions and second-chance points.

lessons.title: Rim protection and shot contests
lessons.objective: Explain rim protection, verticality and a good contest.

payload.prompt: What does rim protection mean?

options.text: Defensive play near the basket including shot-blocking, altering shots and discouraging drives.
Guarding only the three-point line.
Fouling players who drive.

explanation.correct: Right. Rim protection is defensive work near the basket. Blocks, altered shots and physical presence all count.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rim protection is defense near the basket: blocking shots, altering shots and making it hard to score inside.

payload.prompt: What is a good shot contest without fouling?

options.text: A defender moving their hand or arm toward the ball to distract the shooter, with hands up and no contact.
Knocking the ball out of the shooter's hands.
Yelling at the shooter to distract them.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A good contest is hands up, moving toward the shot, no contact. It is hard to make when contested.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A shot contest is hands up and moving toward the ball without fouling. Distance and hands-up matter.

payload.prompt: What is a shot block?

options.text: A defensive action where a defender swats a shot away before it reaches the basket.
Fouling a shooter.
Preventing someone from taking a shot.

explanation.correct: Right. A block is clean swatting of the shot. It is a great defensive play tracked as a statistic.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A block is swatting the ball away when a shooter releases it, before it hits the rim.

payload.prompt: Tap the area where a rim protector defends (near the basket in the paint).

diagram.alt: A basketball court showing defensive areas near the basket.

explanation.correct: Yes! The paint is where rim protectors work. They guard close to the basket and block shots.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rim protectors work in the paint and near the basket to block shots and prevent layups.

payload.question: What is she saying about their defense?

options.text: The team has a great center or defender stopping shots near the basket.
The team is protected from rain.
The basket is rim-shaped.
The team protects the rim with a cover.

payload.translation: She is praising the team's defense near the basket, especially shot-blocking and altering shots inside.

followUps.line: Yeah, he is a beast on defense.
followUps.why: You recognize that a strong rim protector is anchoring the defense.

followUps.line: Does that change their whole defense?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking how the rim protector impacts the entire defensive scheme.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rim protection is just good defense in the paint, especially blocking and altering shots.

lessons.title: Steals, pressure and traps
lessons.objective: Describe pressing, trapping and why gambling for steals is risky.

payload.prompt: What is a steal in basketball?

options.text: A defensive action where a player takes the ball away from an opponent without it being a rebound or turnover.
Taking a timeout when not allowed.
Scoring without being seen by the other team.

explanation.correct: Right. A steal is taking the ball directly from an opponent. It is a highly valued defensive stat.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A steal is when you take the ball away from an opponent during play, counted as a defensive stat.

payload.prompt: What is a full-court press?

options.text: Aggressive defense applied across the entire court to trap the ball handler before half court, forcing turnovers.
Hugging the baseline while defending.
Pressing clothes during a timeout.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A full-court press attacks the ball handler from baseline to baseline, trying to force steals and turnovers.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A full-court press is aggressive defense all over the court, attempting to trap and force turnovers.

payload.prompt: Why is gambling for steals risky?

options.text: Leaving your assigned opponent to go for steals leaves gaps, and skilled offenses punish that by scoring easily.
The referee will call a foul.
You might get hurt chasing the ball.

explanation.correct: Right. Gambling for steals means leaving your player open. If the steal fails, the offense has an easy basket.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Gambling for steals leaves your assignment open. If you do not get the steal, you get beaten.

payload.prompt: The ball handler drives toward the sideline. Your teammate is there. Should you trap or stay home on your player?

options.text: Trap: both of you converge on the driver to force a turnover.
Stay: stay on your player so no one is open.

explanation.correct: Trap is right in this case. The sideline is your friend; the ball handler has nowhere to go. A trap here can force a turnover.
explanation.incorrect: Staying home is safer but the sideline makes this a great trap opportunity. When you have the sideline as a wall, trap the ball handler.

payload.question: What is she calling for?

options.text: Two defenders should converge on the ball handler in the corner to force a turnover.
Push him into the corner of the gymnasium.
Put him in timeout.
Trap the basketball.

payload.translation: She is calling a defensive trap: two defenders should double-team the ball handler in the corner, which has limited escape routes.

followUps.why: You recognize that traps in tight spaces aim to create turnovers.

followUps.line: Someone has to cover the dump-out.
followUps.why: A good follow-up about rotation responsibility when a trap is set.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A trap is just two defenders covering one ball handler. Corner traps are common because there is no escape.

lessons.title: Transition defense and the fast break
lessons.objective: Read numbers advantages and why getting back matters.

payload.prompt: What is transition defense?

options.text: Defensive play immediately after a change of possession, before the opponent sets up a half-court offense.
Switching defenders on a screen.
Changing to zone defense.

explanation.correct: Right. Transition is the scramble from turnover to offense starting. You have seconds to get back and set up.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Transition defense is stopping the offense before they get organized in half court. Speed matters here.

payload.prompt: What is a fast break?

options.text: An offensive attack with a numerical advantage before the defense sets, typically resulting in an easy basket.
Breaking quickly into a sprint without the ball.
A foul called on someone running too fast.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A fast break is a quick offensive surge with more players attacking than defenders. Easy scores come from breaks.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A fast break is when the offense has a numbers advantage (like 3-on-2) and gets an easy basket.

payload.prompt: Three offensive players are heading down the court toward two defenders. Is this a numbers advantage?

scene.alt: Three offensive players rushing toward two defenders.

explanation.correct: Right. Three on two is a numbers advantage for the offense. They have more players, so an easy basket usually results.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Three players attacking two defenders is a clear numbers advantage for the offense.

payload.prompt: After a turnover, a defender sprints back to the basket to help on a fast-breaking offensive player. Is this transition defense?

scene.alt: A defender running back to defend on a fast break.

explanation.correct: Correct. Sprinting back and getting set is exactly what transition defense is. Speed is key.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. That defender is executing transition defense by getting back and setting up to stop the fast break.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Get back, they are in transition.

payload.question: What is she yelling?

options.text: The team should sprint back to defense quickly because the opponent is starting a fast-paced offensive attack.
Get back in the car.
Step backwards during the play.
Go back in time.

payload.translation: She is calling an urgent defensive alert: the opponent has numbers and momentum on a fast break, so defenders must race back immediately to set up before they score an easy basket.

followUps.why: You recognize the numbers disadvantage and the urgency needed.

followUps.line: Somebody has to cut them off at the rim.
followUps.why: A good follow-up about stopping the easy basket.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Transition means the other team is attacking fast after a turnover or rebound. Get back!
